conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ve been reviewing why you came in tonight. You were having shortness of breath, flushing, and itching after your pulmonologist visit, is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. It felt just like my usual mast cell crisis. I tried Benadryl but threw it up. I was scared—I needed help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. You were given IV Benadryl, Ativan, and Dilaudid in the ER, which helped a bit. But your vitals are stable—no fever, your blood pressure is normal, and oxygen levels are good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I still feel awful. I’m short of breath and itchy. Why wouldn’t I need those IV meds again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve spoken with your allergist and your PCP. They agree that without signs of anaphylaxis—like low blood pressure or swelling—this doesn’t meet the criteria for your emergency mast cell plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’ve always used that plan when I feel like this. I don’t understand why it’s being taken away now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not being taken away, but we need to make sure it’s used only when truly needed. IV narcotics and benzodiazepines don’t actually treat mast cell activation and may even worsen it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So you think I’m just asking for pain meds? That’s not fair. I’m in real pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m not saying that. You clearly have chronic pain and complex conditions. But we want to manage this safely. Your PCP agreed you can have IV Phenergan and oral Benadryl for nausea and itching, but not IV opioids or Ativan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fine. But I was told last time to get a pain plan from my pain doctor. I never got that form. No one explained it clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. We’ve contacted your pain specialist. Moving forward, you’ll need a written plan so hospitals know when IV meds are appropriate. We’re faxing this discharge summary to them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your chest X-ray shows your pneumonia is improving. No new infections. Blood cultures were negative, so no antibiotics are needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But my calcium was high, right? Should we worry about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your calcium is mildly elevated at 11.2. Albumin is normal, so it’s not a lab artifact. We started IV fluids, but you chose to stop early. Please follow up with your doctor to check your parathyroid hormone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just wanted to go home. But I’ll make the appointment. What about the lung and spleen spots from my last CT?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The lung nodule and splenic lesions are unchanged. You’ll need a follow-up CT in six months and an outpatient ultrasound of the spleen. We’ll send referrals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been off all IV meds since 4 a.m., and you’re breathing comfortably. Your skin isn’t flushed or itchy. We think you’re ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m just supposed to go back to my oral meds? What if this happens again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your regular oral hydromorphone, lorazepam, and Benadryl as needed. But next time, bring your written pain plan. If you don’t have one, see your pain doctor soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. But I hope you’re not dismissing me when I’m really struggling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not dismissing you. We take your symptoms seriously. But we need to balance safety and long-term care. We’re here to help coordinate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll follow up with my doctors. Thank you for explaining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ve updated your duloxetine to 60 mg daily for mood support, and added gabapentin for nerve-related pain. Take all meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And I’ll keep using my nasal cromolyn and omeprazole like before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Same for methotrexate—take your weekly dose at home. You were due for etanercept, so schedule that injection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I feel better already just knowing what’s next.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. Discharge is set for noon. A nurse will go over your instructions and prescriptions before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’ll make sure to follow up on everything.
